explanations.answer: What must happen after these things
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The voice says, “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.” So John, the one seeing all this, isn't getting a history lesson. He's getting a look at what's ahead.

Creation does show up later in this scene, friend, when the elders say God created all things. But the voice isn't pointing backward. It promises to show John “…what must happen after these things.” That's a door opening toward what comes next.

explanations.answer: Where the garden of Eden stood
explanations.explanation: A garden tour would be nice, but nobody's handing out maps here. The garden of Eden is back in Genesis (Genesis 2:8), and this door opens the other direction. The voice promises John “…what must happen after these things.”

Lightning gets the headlines, but the verse gives the whole show: “From the throne came flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder.” Flashes for the eyes, rumblings and peals for the ears. I'd be holding my mustache over my ears about now.
I see where you're going, friend. Lightning and a storm usually come with wind and rain. But this verse doesn't mention either one. It says “…flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder.”

Smoke and hail make a dramatic picture, baker, but they aren't in this verse. What comes from the throne is “…flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder.” The seven torches of fire burn before the throne, but that's a separate detail. Smoke and hail didn't make the list.

That's it, friend. John sees “…something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal.” Notice he says something like. He's reaching for words to describe what he sees. I've never gotten my oven door that clear.
Dark is the opposite of what John describes, friend. He says the sea of glass is “…as clear as crystal.” You can see right through it. Nothing murky about that picture.

Thunder and lightning were just in the last verse, so I get why storm clouds came to mind. But John describes the sea in front of the throne as “…as clear as crystal.” Clear, not gray. It's a different picture altogether.
Not quite, baker. The creatures say God “…was and is and is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). That's past, present and future in one breath. Long ago is only the first third of it.

That's right, friend. The creatures say “…who was and is and is to come!” So yes, He was, but He also is, and He is to come. Past, present and future, and they never stop saying it day and night. I lose my breath after one sneeze.

True, baker. Whenever the living creatures give glory, honor and thanks to the One on the throne, the twenty-four elders fall down before Him. Then they worship Him who lives forever and ever. Notice the word whenever. It happens every time, not just once.

This one is true, friend, so it's no trick. The verse says that whenever the living creatures give glory, honor and thanks, the twenty-four elders fall down before the One seated on the throne. Then they worship Him who lives forever and ever. Whenever means every time the creatures give glory.

That's what the elders do. They “…cast their crowns before the throne…” while they worship. Those are golden crowns going down in front of the throne. I'd have trouble letting go of my hat, and mine is only cloth.
I can picture that, friend, but nothing in the verse goes upward. The elders “…cast their crowns before the throne…” The crowns go down in front of the throne, not up in the air.

explanations.answer: Hand them to the living creatures
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, since the living creatures are right there. But the verse never has anybody passing a crown to them. The elders “…cast their crowns before the throne…” and that's where the crowns end up.

Yes, baker. The elders say, “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things…” They say He's worthy because He created everything. Their praise starts with who made it all.

Judged is a big word, friend, but it isn't the one the elders use. They say He's worthy “…for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.” Creating is the reason they give in this verse.
Naming matters, baker. The Millers carved Dorin into my handle, and I still carry it. But the elders don't say named. They say, “…for You created all things…”

Nobody, friend. The text says “…no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it.” That covers heaven, earth and under the earth. The answer to the angel's question is a long, quiet nobody.

An elder does speak up in this passage, but not to open the scroll. He talks to John and points to someone else. The text says “…no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it.”

The mighty angel is the one asking the question, friend. He's the one proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?” The text says “…no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it.” That includes him.

True, baker. John says, “And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it.” John is the one writing this down, and he tells us about his own tears. He doesn't hide it.

John does weep, friend, so this one is true. He says, “And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it.” John, who is seeing all this, tells us himself. The tears come right after the angel's question gets no answer.

Judah it is, baker. The elder says, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals.” John was crying over a closed scroll, and the elder says someone has triumphed to open it. That's one big turn in a single verse.
Levi is a real tribe, friend. He was one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 29:34). But the elder says “…the Lion of the tribe of Judah…” and that's the name to remember here.

Dan was another of Jacob's sons (Genesis 30:6), so it's a fair guess. But the elder says, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed…” The tribe named in the verse is Judah.

Yes, friend. John writes, “Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne…” The elder had just said Lion, and John looks and sees a Lamb. Standing, though He appeared slain.

explanations.answer: A lion with a golden crown
explanations.explanation: The elder did say Lion, so that guess makes sense. But what John sees is “…a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne…” No crown on a lion in this verse. The text shows a Lamb.

Angels are in this scene, baker, and the mighty angel was just asking the question. But nobody here holds a sword. John sees “…a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne…”

Not quite, friend. The Lamb doesn't wait for anybody. The verse says, “And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne.” The Lamb comes and takes it Himself. The mighty angel doesn't carry it over.
That's right, baker. The verse says, “And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne.” The Lamb comes and takes the scroll Himself. Nobody brings it to Him.

Prayers, baker. John says they're holding “…golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” So the incense in those bowls stands for the prayers of the saints. Nothing about those prayers is thrown away here.
John did weep back in verse 4, so tears are a fair guess. But the verse says the bowls are full of incense, “…which are the prayers of the saints.” The bowls hold prayers, not tears.
Golden bowls do look like they could hold gifts, friend. But John says the incense is “…the prayers of the saints.” That's the word he uses.

explanations.answer: He was slain and purchased people for God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the song. They sing, “Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God…” The song gives what He did as the reason He's worthy. The Lamb who was slain is the One who takes the scroll.

explanations.answer: He is the oldest one in all of heaven
explanations.explanation: The song never mentions His age, friend. It says He's worthy “…because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God…” The reason is what He did, not how long He's been around.

explanations.answer: The mighty angel chose Him to open it
explanations.explanation: The mighty angel only asks the question, baker. Nobody in the song says he chose anybody. They sing, “…because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God…” That's the reason they give.

explanations.answer: Every tribe and tongue and nation
explanations.explanation: That's the list, baker. The song says He purchased people “…from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.” That's a wide circle. Every tribe, every tongue, every people and every nation.

I get the thought, friend, since the elder called Him the Lion of the tribe of Judah. But the song says the people He purchased come “…from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.” Every tribe, not Judah alone.
No city is named in that song, friend. It says He purchased people “…from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.” That's far wider than one city.

Not quite, friend. John says, “And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying…” That's heaven, earth, under the earth and the sea. My own choir is me humming at the ovens, so I'm impressed.

Right, baker. John says he heard “…every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them…” So it isn't only heaven. Every creature joins the praise to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb.
